signs.note: Sahih Muslim lists ten major signs before the Hour without fixing their order. This follows a common order given by the scholars.

items.name: The sun rises from the west
A fire from Yemen drives people to their gathering

villains.name: Iblis
villains.title: The one who refused
villains.deed: A jinn raised among the angels. When Allah commanded them to bow to Adam, he refused out of pride, then swore to mislead Adam's children until the Last Day.
villains.end: Given respite until the Day of Judgement. His end is the Fire, with everyone who follows him (38:85).
villains.note: Named 11 times in the Quran.
villains.lesson: Pride in what you were made from, not in what you do, was the first sin.

villains.name: Qabil
villains.title: The first murderer
villains.undone: A crow that showed him his shame
villains.deed: A son of Adam who killed his brother Habil out of envy, after Habil's offering was accepted and his was not.
villains.end: He became one of the regretful. The Prophet ﷺ said every unjust killing carries a share of blame for him, because he made killing a way.
villains.note: The Quran tells the story of 'the two sons of Adam' (5:27–31); the names come from the commentators. The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.
villains.lesson: Envy can turn a brother into a stranger, and then into a victim.

villains.name: The people of Nuh
villains.title: Who mocked the ark
villains.relied: Their idols: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr
villains.deed: Nuh called them for 950 years, by night and by day, in public and in private. They put their fingers in their ears, called him a madman, and mocked him as he built the ark.
villains.end: The sky opened and the earth burst with springs. All but the few on the ark were drowned (54:11-12).
villains.note: Ibn Abbas said the five idols were named after righteous men whose statues were later worshipped (Sahih al-Bukhari 4920).
villains.lesson: Idol worship began with honouring good men too much, then bowing to their images.

villains.name: The son of Nuh
villains.title: Who would not board the ark
villains.relied: A mountain to keep him from the water
villains.deed: As the flood rose, Nuh called to his son to come aboard and not stay with the disbelievers. He refused, saying he would climb a mountain to escape the water.
villains.end: A wave came between them and he drowned. When Nuh pleaded for him, Allah told him his son was not of his family, for his deeds were not righteous (11:46).
villains.note: The Quran does not name him. Commentators call him Kan'an; some say Yam.
villains.lesson: Even a prophet's son is saved only by his own faith.

villains.name: The wife of Nuh
villains.title: Who betrayed a prophet at home
villains.deed: She lived with a righteous prophet but did not share his faith. The commentators say she told people he was mad and warned the leaders about those who believed.
villains.end: The Quran gives her as an example for those who disbelieve: 'Enter the Fire with those who enter' (66:10).
villains.note: The Quran does not name her. Ibn Abbas explained that her betrayal was of faith, not of the marriage. Some commentators name her Wa'ilah; the reports differ.
villains.lesson: Living beside the righteous saves no one who turns away.

villains.name: The people of Ad
villains.title: Who asked who was stronger
villains.relied: Their strength and their towering buildings
villains.deed: A mighty people of the sand dunes who built monuments on every height and fortresses as if they would live for ever. They called Hud a fool and asked, 'Who is greater than us in strength?'
villains.end: They saw a cloud and cheered at the rain. It was a furious wind that blew for seven nights and eight days and left them like hollow palm trunks (69:6-7).
villains.note: Their land, al-Ahqaf, is placed by most commentators in southern Arabia between Yemen and Oman.
villains.lesson: Strength that forgets the One who gave it is weakness waiting to happen.

villains.name: Shaddad ibn Ad
villains.title: Builder of Iram, in legend
villains.relied: A city of pillars to rival Paradise
villains.undone: Death at the gate, in the story
villains.deed: Storytellers say a king of Ad built Iram, a city of gold and lofty pillars meant to rival Paradise, and died before he could enter it.
villains.end: The Quran says only that Ad of Iram, 'who had lofty pillars', were destroyed with the other nations that transgressed (89:6-13).
villains.note: The tale of Shaddad and his golden city is not in the Quran or authentic hadith. Ibn Kathir in his tafsir treats it as a fable of the storytellers. Most commentators take Iram as a tribe or a city of Ad.
villains.lesson: The Quran keeps the lesson of Iram, not the gold of its walls.

villains.name: Qudar ibn Salif
villains.title: The most wretched of Thamud
villains.deed: Thamud were given a she-camel as a sign and told not to harm her. Qudar volunteered to kill her, and his people cheered him on.
villains.end: Salih warned them of three days. Then a single blast struck Thamud, and they lay dead in their carved homes.
villains.note: The Quran calls him 'the most wretched of them'. Sahih al-Bukhari describes him as a strong, powerful man; his name comes from the commentators.
villains.lesson: Those who cheer a crime share in it: all of Thamud fell for one man's deed.

villains.name: The nine of Thamud
villains.title: Who plotted to kill Salih by night
villains.deed: Nine clan leaders of al-Hijr spread corruption in the land. They swore an oath by Allah to kill Salih and his family by night, then tell his heirs they had seen nothing.
villains.end: Allah destroyed them and their people, and left their houses empty as a sign (27:51-52).
villains.note: The commentators count Qudar, who killed the she-camel, among the nine.
villains.lesson: They planned a plan and Allah planned a plan, while they did not perceive (27:50).

villains.name: The people of the Well
villains.title: A nation lost to history
villains.deed: Named twice beside Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh among the nations who denied their messengers. Some commentators say they threw their prophet into a well.
villains.end: They were destroyed with the others, 'and many generations between them' (25:38).
villains.note: Who they were is not known. The commentators give different views: a remnant of Thamud, a town in Yamamah, or a people further east.
villains.lesson: Most of history's wrongdoers are not remembered by name, only by how they ended.

villains.name: Namrud
villains.title: The king who argued about Allah
villains.deed: A king who claimed power over life and death. Ibrahim answered: Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west. Ibrahim's people then threw him into a fire.
villains.end: The Quran says he was left speechless. The fire was made cool for Ibrahim (21:69).
villains.note: The Quran does not name him; the early commentators identify him as Namrud.
villains.lesson: Power over people is not power over creation.

villains.name: The people of Lut
villains.title: Who made a new sin their custom
villains.deed: The towns of Sodom were the first to make immorality between men their way, and they robbed travellers on the road. When Lut warned them, they threatened to throw him out for wanting to stay pure.
villains.end: At dawn their towns were turned upside down and rained on with stones of layered clay (11:82).
villains.note: Their story is told in at least eight surahs. Their land is placed by the Dead Sea.
villains.lesson: When purity is mocked as a crime, a people has lost its way.

villains.name: The wife of Lut
villains.title: Who sided with her people
villains.deed: She lived in a prophet's house but sided with the people of Sodom. The commentators say she let them know when guests came to Lut.
villains.end: Lut was told to leave by night with his family, except his wife: 'she will be struck by that which strikes them' (11:81).
villains.note: The Quran does not name her. Some commentators name her Wahilah; the reports differ.
villains.lesson: Living beside the truth is not the same as following it.

villains.name: The people of Madyan
villains.title: Who cheated on the scales
villains.deed: A trading people who gave short measure, cheated on the scales and blocked the roads. When Shuayb called them to honesty, they mocked his prayer and threatened to drive him out.
villains.end: An earthquake seized them and they lay fallen in their homes (7:91). The Quran also tells of 'the day of the black cloud' (26:189).
villains.note: Whether Madyan and 'the companions of the thicket' (al-Aykah) were one people or two, the commentators differ.
villains.lesson: Cheating in small measures is how a whole people falls.

villains.name: Firaun
villains.title: The Pharaoh of Musa
villains.relied: His kingdom and 'these rivers flowing beneath me'
villains.deed: Ruler of Egypt who enslaved the Children of Israil, killed their newborn sons, and declared himself their highest lord.
villains.end: He drowned in the sea while chasing Musa. He declared belief at his last breath, too late, and his body was kept as a sign for later generations (10:90–92).
villains.note: Named 74 times in the Quran, more than any other villain.
villains.lesson: Whatever you rely on instead of Allah can become the thing that drowns you.

villains.name: Haman
villains.title: Pharaoh's minister
villains.undone: The same sea as his master
villains.deed: Pharaoh's chief minister and builder, ordered to raise a tower of baked brick so Pharaoh could 'look at the god of Musa'.
villains.end: Destroyed with Pharaoh and their armies (28:8, 29:39).
villains.note: Named 6 times in the Quran.
villains.lesson: Building a tyrant's lie means sharing its end.

villains.name: The chiefs of Firaun
villains.title: Who urged him on
villains.deed: The nobles of Pharaoh's court called Musa a magician, gathered sorcerers against him, and pushed Pharaoh to kill the sons of Bani Israil again.
villains.end: They drowned with Pharaoh and his armies.
villains.note: The Quran calls them al-mala', 'the eminent'. One believing man from Pharaoh's own family stood up against them (40:28).
villains.lesson: Those who urge a tyrant on share his end.

villains.name: Qarun
villains.title: The richest man of his people
villains.deed: One of Musa's own people, so rich that the keys to his treasure were a burden for strong men. He paraded his wealth and claimed he had earned it by his own knowledge.
villains.end: The earth swallowed him and his house (28:81).
villains.note: Named 4 times in the Quran.
villains.lesson: Wealth is a test, not proof that you deserve it.

villains.name: The Samiri
villains.title: Maker of the golden calf
villains.relied: A calf of gold that made a sound
villains.undone: Exile: 'no touching' for the rest of his life
villains.deed: While Musa was on the mountain receiving the Tawrat, he melted the people's gold into a lowing calf and told them it was their god.
villains.end: Musa cast him out, to say 'no touching' for the rest of his life. The calf was burned and scattered in the sea (20:97).
villains.note: Named 3 times in Surah Ta-Ha.
villains.lesson: An idol made of gold is still an idol.

said.from: "I saw what they did not see

villains.name: The killer in the story of the cow
villains.title: The murder Allah brought to light
villains.deed: A man of Bani Israil was found killed and the people argued over who did it. The commentators say his own nephew killed him for his inheritance, then came demanding blood money.
villains.end: Allah ordered a cow to be slaughtered. The dead man was struck with a part of it, came to life, and named his killer (2:72-73).
villains.note: The Quran tells of the killing and the cow; the nephew and the inheritance come from the commentators.
villains.lesson: Allah was to bring out what they were concealing (2:72).

villains.name: The king who seized ships
villains.title: Whom al-Khidr outwitted
villains.deed: Al-Khidr made a hole in a poor family's boat, and Musa protested. Al-Khidr later explained that a king ahead was seizing every sound ship by force.
villains.end: The damaged boat was passed over, and the poor sailors kept their living.
villains.note: The Quran does not name him. A narration in Sahih al-Bukhari mentions that some called him Hadad ibn Badad; the name is not from the Prophet ﷺ.
villains.lesson: What looks like loss can be protection: the boat was saved by its flaw.

villains.name: Bal'am ibn Ba'ura
villains.title: The scholar who threw off the signs
villains.relied: Knowledge, and prayers that were answered
villains.deed: The Quran tells of a man given Allah's signs who slipped out of them and followed his desires. Many commentators say he was Bal'am, a man of knowledge who was paid to pray against Musa and his people.
villains.end: The Quran likens him to a dog that pants whether you chase it or leave it (7:176).
villains.note: The Quran does not name him. Ibn Masud and Ibn Abbas are reported to say he was Bal'am; others said Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt. The name and story come from the commentators.
villains.lesson: Knowledge without obedience can bring a man lower than the ignorant.

villains.name: Jalut
villains.title: The giant
villains.deed: Commander of the army that oppressed Bani Israil. Many of Talut's soldiers lost heart at the sight of him.
villains.end: Killed by the young Dawud (2:251).
villains.note: Named 3 times in the Quran.
villains.lesson: How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah (2:249).

villains.name: The Sabbath-breakers
villains.title: The town by the sea
villains.relied: A trick to get around the law
villains.deed: A town of Bani Israil by the sea was forbidden to fish on the Sabbath, and the fish came openly on that day. So they set their nets on the Sabbath and pulled them in the next day, calling it obedience.
villains.end: Those who warned them were saved. The rest were told: 'Be apes, despised' (7:166).
villains.note: Ibn Abbas is reported to place the town at Aylah, near today's Aqaba. Most commentators say the change was real; Mujahid said it was of their hearts. Some link them to 5:78, cursed 'by the tongue of Dawud'.
villains.lesson: A trick that keeps the letter of the law and breaks its purpose is still disobedience.

villains.name: The killers of the prophets
villains.title: Who killed the messengers sent to them
villains.relied: Rejecting whatever they did not like
villains.deed: The Quran says again and again that some of Bani Israil killed prophets without right, whenever a messenger brought what their desires did not want.
villains.end: They were covered with humiliation and returned with anger from Allah (2:61).
villains.note: The Quran blames those who did it, not a whole people: 'They are not all the same' (3:113). The commentators count Zakariya and Yahya among the prophets killed.
villains.lesson: Killing the messenger never killed the message.

villains.name: Herod Antipas
villains.title: The king who killed Yahya
villains.deed: Ruler of Galilee under Rome. Yahya told him that his marriage to his brother's wife was forbidden, and the king had him beheaded.
villains.end: Rome stripped him of his lands in 39 CE and sent him into exile in Gaul, where he died.
villains.note: The Quran praises Yahya but does not tell of his death. Muslim historians tell of a king who killed him over a forbidden marriage, and Ibn Kathir reports his head is buried in Damascus; the name Herod comes from the Gospels and Josephus.
villains.lesson: Yahya lost his life and kept his honour; peace be upon him the day he died (19:15).

villains.name: Those who plotted against Isa
villains.title: Who boasted of the crucifixion
villains.deed: Leaders who rejected Isa plotted to have him killed, and then boasted that they had killed the Messiah.
villains.end: The Quran says they did not kill him or crucify him; another was made to resemble him, and Allah raised Isa up to Himself (4:157-158).
villains.note: Who was made to resemble Isa is not in the Quran. Some reports in the commentaries say a disciple volunteered; others say it was the one who betrayed him. These are reports, not certainty.
villains.lesson: They planned and Allah planned, and Allah is the best of planners (3:54).

villains.name: The people of the town
villains.title: Who killed the man who came running
villains.relied: Calling the messengers a bad omen
villains.deed: Two messengers came to a town, then a third. The people called them a bad omen and threatened to stone them. A man came running from the far end of the town to defend them, and they killed him.
villains.end: One shout struck them and they were extinguished (36:29). The man was told: 'Enter Paradise' (36:26).
villains.note: Many commentators say the town was Antioch and the man was Habib, but the Quran names neither. Ibn Kathir doubted Antioch, since it was among the first cities to believe in Isa.
villains.lesson: One man who speaks up for the truth outweighs a town that silences him.

said.from: "Indeed, we consider you a bad omen

villains.name: Daqyanus
villains.title: The king the sleepers fled
villains.deed: A pagan king who forced his people to worship idols and punished believers. A few young men fled his city and hid in a cave, where Allah put them to sleep.
villains.end: When they woke, his reign was long gone and the city had come to believe.
villains.note: The Quran does not name the king. The commentators call him Daqyanus, often taken to be the Roman emperor Decius, who persecuted Christians around 250 CE.
villains.lesson: The tyrant ruled for a few years; the young men's story is recited for ever.

villains.name: Amr ibn Luhayy
villains.title: Who brought idols to Arabia
villains.relied: His rank as lord of Makkah
villains.undone: What the Prophet ﷺ was shown
villains.deed: A chief of Khuza'ah who ruled Makkah. He brought idols from Syria, set them around the Kaaba, and invented rules for camels set loose in the idols' names, changing the religion of Ibrahim.
villains.end: The Prophet ﷺ said he saw him in the Fire dragging his intestines; he was the first to set camels loose for the idols.
villains.note: The vision is in Sahih al-Bukhari. That he brought the idol Hubal from Syria is from Ibn Ishaq.
villains.lesson: One leader's innovation can mislead a people for centuries.

villains.name: Dhu Nuwas
villains.title: King of the trench
villains.relied: Fire and the throne of Himyar
villains.undone: An army from across the sea
villains.deed: King of Himyar in Yemen who dug trenches of fire at Najran and burned the believers who would not give up their faith.
villains.end: An Abyssinian army took his kingdom. Historians report he rode his horse into the sea.
villains.note: Surah al-Buruj tells of 'the companions of the trench'; Ibn Ishaq and the commentators connect it to Dhu Nuwas. Sahih Muslim 3005 tells of a boy, a monk and a king that ends at a trench of fire; scholars differ whether that king was Dhu Nuwas or an earlier one.
villains.lesson: The believers lost their lives and won; the king kept his and lost everything.

villains.name: Abraha
villains.title: Lord of the elephant
villains.deed: Abyssinian ruler of Yemen who marched on Makkah with war elephants to destroy the Kaaba, in the year the Prophet ﷺ was born.
villains.end: Flocks of birds pelted his army with stones of baked clay, leaving them 'like eaten straw', as Abd al-Muttalib had said: 'The House has a Lord who will protect it.' Abraha died of his wounds soon after reaching Sana'a.
villains.note: Surah al-Fil tells of 'the companions of the elephant'; his name comes from Ibn Ishaq and the commentators.
villains.lesson: The House has a Lord who protects it.

villains.name: Abu Lahab
villains.title: The Prophet's own uncle
villains.relied: His wealth and his family name
villains.undone: A disease his own family feared to touch
villains.deed: When the Prophet ﷺ first called Quraysh from Mount Safa, his uncle cursed him. He followed him through the markets telling people not to listen, and his wife Umm Jamil scattered thorns on his path.
villains.end: A surah promised his ruin while he was still alive. He died of a disease a week after Badr, and his family left his body for days in fear of it.
villains.note: The only enemy of the Prophet ﷺ named in the Quran. The scene at Safa is in Sahih al-Bukhari; his death is from Ibn Ishaq.
villains.lesson: Being family to the Prophet ﷺ saved no one who rejected him.

villains.name: Umm Jamil
villains.title: The carrier of firewood
villains.deed: Arwa bint Harb, wife of Abu Lahab. She scattered thorns on the Prophet's ﷺ path and made up verses insulting him.
villains.end: The Quran named her fate with her husband's: a rope of palm fibre around her neck (111:4-5). She died a disbeliever.
villains.note: The Quran calls her 'the carrier of firewood' without naming her. Her name, the thorns and her verses come from Ibn Ishaq and the commentators. Her brother Abu Sufyan later became a Companion.
villains.lesson: She heard her own fate recited and still chose it.

villains.name: Abu Jahl
villains.title: Leader of the persecution
villains.deed: Amr ibn Hisham led Quraysh's war on Islam. He killed Sumayyah, the first martyr, enforced the boycott, and swore to trample the Prophet's ﷺ neck while he prayed.
villains.end: Killed at Badr. Two teenage boys of the Ansar struck him down, and Ibn Masud finished him.
villains.note: Sahih Muslim reports that the closing verses of Surah al-Alaq came down about him. His death at Badr is in Sahih al-Bukhari; the killing of Sumayyah is from the Seerah.
villains.lesson: The arrogant are often brought down by those they looked down on.

said.from: "O Allah, if this should be the truth

villains.name: Umayyah ibn Khalaf
villains.title: Torturer of Bilal
villains.undone: That man's cry on the battlefield
villains.deed: He laid his slave Bilal on burning sand under a heavy rock to make him renounce Islam. Bilal only answered: 'One. One.'
villains.end: Killed at Badr, after Bilal recognised him on the battlefield.
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari; the torture of Bilal is from Ibn Ishaq.
villains.lesson: Bilal, the slave he tortured, lived to call the adhan from the roof of the Kaaba.

villains.name: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah
villains.title: Who called the Quran magic
villains.undone: Death, still refusing what he knew was true
villains.deed: A rich chief of Quraysh who admitted the Quran moved him. To keep his standing, he told Quraysh to call it magic and the Prophet ﷺ a sorcerer.
villains.end: He died in Makkah still rejecting it. Surah al-Muddaththir answered him: 'I will drive him into Saqar' (74:26).
villains.note: The commentators agree that 74:11–26 is about him.
villains.lesson: Knowing the truth and rejecting it for status is the oldest trap.

villains.name: al-As ibn Wa'il
villains.title: Who called the Prophet ﷺ cut off
villains.deed: A chief of Quraysh who mocked the Prophet ﷺ when his sons died, calling him 'cut off', with no one to carry his name. He refused to pay Khabbab his wage, saying he would pay him in the next life.
villains.end: Surah al-Kawthar answered him: 'Your enemy is the one cut off' (108:3). He died a disbeliever in Makkah, while his son Amr became a Companion.
villains.note: Khabbab's story and the coming of 19:77 are in Sahih al-Bukhari. That 108:3 is about him comes from the commentators.
villains.lesson: The Prophet's ﷺ name is called in every adhan; few have heard of the man who called him cut off.

villains.name: The mockers of Makkah
villains.title: Who laughed at the Prophet ﷺ
villains.deed: A handful of Quraysh chiefs made a sport of mocking the Prophet ﷺ in the streets and at the Kaaba, and laughed and winked at the believers as they passed.
villains.end: Allah promised: 'Indeed, We are sufficient for you against the mockers' (15:95). The commentators say each of them died soon after, in disgrace.
villains.note: The commentators name al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth and al-Harith ibn Qays.
villains.lesson: Mockery is the weapon of those who have no argument.

villains.name: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith
villains.title: Who told stories against the Quran
villains.deed: He learned the tales of Rustam and the kings of Persia. When the Prophet ﷺ recited the Quran, he would sit after him and tell them, asking who told the better stories, and called the Quran 'legends of the former peoples'.
villains.end: Captured at Badr and executed on the road back to Madinah.
villains.note: Ibn Ishaq and the commentators connect 8:31 and 31:6 to him. Some add 8:32, though al-Bukhari reports those words from Abu Jahl.
villains.lesson: Entertainment used to drown out the truth is the 'amusement of speech' the Quran warns of (31:6).

villains.name: Uqbah ibn Abi Muayt
villains.title: Who attacked the Prophet ﷺ in prayer
villains.deed: He dropped a camel's entrails on the Prophet's ﷺ back while he prostrated at the Kaaba, and once twisted a cloth around his neck until Abu Bakr pulled him away.
villains.end: Captured at Badr and executed on the road back to Madinah.
villains.note: Bukhari 240 tells of the entrails without naming the man; the Seerah names him as Uqbah. The choking is in Bukhari 3856, his execution in the Seerah of Ibn Ishaq. The commentators say 25:27 is about him.
villains.lesson: Choose your friends: 25:27–29 is about a man who followed the wrong one.

villains.name: Utbah ibn Rabi'ah
villains.title: Who came out first at Badr
villains.deed: A respected elder of Quraysh. He once offered the Prophet ﷺ wealth, rule or a cure if he would give up his message, and heard the opening of Surah Fussilat in reply. At Badr he came out to duel with his brother Shaybah and his son al-Walid.
villains.end: All three were killed in the duels that opened Badr. Abu Dharr swore that 22:19, 'These are two adversaries', came down about them.
villains.note: Abu Dharr's oath about 22:19 is reported by al-Bukhari; the offer and Fussilat are from Ibn Ishaq. His daughter Hind and his son Abu Hudhayfah became Muslims.
villains.lesson: He heard the Quran and admitted its power, but would not leave his people's way.

villains.name: Ubayy ibn Khalaf
villains.title: Who crumbled a bone
villains.relied: A horse he fattened for the day
villains.undone: A graze from the Prophet's ﷺ spear
villains.deed: Brother of Umayyah ibn Khalaf. He crumbled an old bone in front of the Prophet ﷺ and asked who could give it life. He swore he would kill the Prophet ﷺ on a horse he was feeding for that day.
villains.end: At Uhud he charged the Prophet ﷺ, who took a spear and grazed his neck. He died of the wound on the way back to Makkah, the only man the Prophet ﷺ killed with his own hand.
villains.note: The commentators say 36:77-79 came down about him; some say al-As ibn Wa'il. His death at Uhud is from Ibn Ishaq.
villains.lesson: He who made them the first time will give them life again (36:79).

villains.name: Abdullah ibn Ubayy
villains.title: Head of the hypocrites
villains.deed: A Madinah chief who was about to be crowned when the Prophet ﷺ arrived. He claimed Islam, then pulled a third of the army back before Uhud and spread the slander against Aisha.
villains.end: He died in 9 AH. The Prophet ﷺ prayed over him out of mercy, and then a verse came forbidding prayer over hypocrites (9:84).
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari records that he said these words and that 9:84 came after his funeral.
villains.lesson: Hypocrisy is the enemy within, and the Quran gives it a whole surah.

villains.name: The hypocrites
villains.title: The enemy within
villains.deed: Men of Madinah who professed Islam while working against it: turning back before Uhud, spreading slander, staying home from Tabuk with excuses, and mocking the believers in private.
villains.end: The Quran exposed them in Surahs al-Baqarah, al-Tawbah and al-Munafiqun, and placed them in the lowest depth of the Fire (4:145).
villains.note: Their head was Abdullah ibn Ubayy. The Prophet ﷺ gave three signs of a hypocrite: lying when he speaks, breaking his promise, and betraying a trust (Sahih al-Bukhari 33).
villains.lesson: The Companions feared hypocrisy in themselves; that fear is a sign of faith.

villains.name: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf
villains.title: The poet who called for war
villains.undone: A night visit from Muhammad ibn Maslamah
villains.deed: A rich chief and poet of Madinah, bound by its covenant. After Badr he rode to Makkah, mourned the dead of Quraysh, urged them to fight again, and wrote verses against the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslim women.
villains.end: The Prophet ﷺ asked who would deal with him, 'for he has harmed Allah and His Messenger'. Muhammad ibn Maslamah and his companions killed him outside his fortress.
villains.note: His killing is in Sahih al-Bukhari. The commentators say 4:51 came down when he told Quraysh their religion was better guided; his journey and poems are from Ibn Ishaq.
villains.lesson: Fulfil every commitment; it will be asked about (17:34).

villains.name: Amir ibn al-Tufayl
villains.title: Who betrayed the seventy reciters
villains.deed: Seventy Companions known for reciting the Quran were sent to teach in Najd. At the well of Ma'unah, Amir ibn al-Tufayl had their envoy Haram ibn Milhan speared from behind, and the tribes he called killed the rest.
villains.end: As the spear struck him, Haram cried: 'I have won, by the Lord of the Kaaba!' Amir later fell ill with a swelling 'like a camel's' and died on his horse, a disbeliever.
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet ﷺ prayed against the tribes of Ri'l and Dhakwan for a month.
villains.lesson: Haram's last words turned a massacre into a victory.

villains.name: Abu Rafi' of Khaybar
villains.title: Who funded the war on Madinah
villains.undone: Abdullah ibn Atik in the dark
villains.deed: Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, a rich merchant of Khaybar, used to harm the Prophet ﷺ and help his enemies against him with his wealth.
villains.end: Abdullah ibn Atik slipped into his fortress at night and killed him, then broke his leg on the stairs. The Prophet ﷺ passed his hand over it and it healed.
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari. The year is disputed: 3, 4 or 6 AH.
villains.lesson: Wealth spent to block the way of Allah becomes a regret (8:36).

villains.name: Huyayy ibn Akhtab
villains.title: Who gathered the Confederates
villains.deed: Chief of Banu Nadir in Madinah. After his tribe was exiled for plotting against the Prophet ﷺ, he went to Makkah and the tribes to raise the army of the Confederates, then persuaded Banu Qurayzah to break their treaty.
villains.end: When the siege failed, he joined Qurayzah in their fortress and was executed with their fighters. His daughter Safiyyah later became a Mother of the Believers.
villains.note: From Ibn Ishaq and al-Waqidi. The commentators say 59:2-4 is about the exile of Banu Nadir.
villains.lesson: They thought their fortresses would protect them from Allah (59:2).

villains.name: Banu Qurayzah
villains.title: The treaty broken at the Trench
villains.deed: A Jewish tribe of Madinah bound by treaty to defend the city. During the siege of the Trench, their leaders broke the treaty and sided with the Confederates, leaving the Muslims open from behind.
villains.end: After the siege lifted they surrendered and asked for the judgement of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, their old ally. He ruled that their fighting men be executed and the rest taken captive.
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari records Sa'd's judgement. The reports differ on how many were killed, and historians still discuss it.
villains.lesson: A treaty is kept in the hour of danger, not only in easy times (8:56).

villains.name: Dhul-Khuwaysirah
villains.title: Who told the Prophet ﷺ to be just
villains.deed: As the Prophet ﷺ shared out wealth, a man of Banu Tamim stood up and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, be just!' The Prophet ﷺ replied: 'Woe to you, who would be just if I were not?'
villains.end: The Prophet ﷺ said that people would come from his kind who recite the Quran but it goes no deeper than their throats, and pass out of Islam as an arrow passes through its game.
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari. Some reports place it at al-Ji'ranah after Hunayn. Scholars see him as the root of the Khawarij.
villains.lesson: Zeal without humility led him to judge the Prophet ﷺ himself.

villains.name: Abu Amir the Monk
villains.title: Behind the mosque of harm
villains.relied: A mosque used as a cover
villains.undone: Revelation, and the fire that followed
villains.deed: An ascetic of Madinah known as 'the monk' who turned against the Prophet ﷺ, fought with Quraysh at Uhud, then went north to seek Byzantine help. His allies built a mosque near Quba as a base for his return.
villains.end: On the way back from Tabuk the Quran exposed the 'mosque of harm', and the Prophet ﷺ had it burned. Abu Amir died in exile in Syria.
villains.note: The commentators agree that 'whoever had warred against Allah and His Messenger before' (9:107) means him. His son Hanzalah died a martyr at Uhud and was washed by the angels.
villains.lesson: A building called a mosque is not one if it was founded to divide (9:108).

villains.name: Musaylimah
villains.title: The Liar
villains.deed: He claimed prophethood in Yamamah and wrote to the Prophet ﷺ offering to share the earth. The reply was addressed 'to Musaylimah the Liar'.
villains.end: Killed at the Battle of Yamamah in 632 by Wahshi, whose spear had once killed Hamzah. Wahshi had since become Muslim and called it his amends.

verse.to: nothing has been inspired to him

villains.note: The Prophet ﷺ saw him in a dream as one of two liars (Sahih al-Bukhari). His death is also in al-Bukhari.
villains.lesson: Claiming to speak for Allah is the greatest lie (6:93).

villains.name: al-Aswad al-Ansi
villains.title: The false prophet of Yemen
villains.undone: A man inside his own palace
villains.deed: He seized Yemen in the Prophet's ﷺ last months, claiming to be a prophet.
villains.end: Killed by Fayruz al-Daylami just before the Prophet ﷺ died.

verse.to: nothing has been inspired to him

villains.note: The other liar of the dream in Sahih al-Bukhari. His death is from al-Tabari.
villains.lesson: No prophet comes after the last Prophet ﷺ, and every false claimant has fallen.

villains.name: Tulayhah al-Asadi
villains.title: The false prophet who came back
villains.relied: Claimed revelations and the tribes of Asad
villains.deed: A chief of Banu Asad who claimed prophethood in the Prophet's ﷺ last year, and led tribes of Najd against Madinah after his death.
villains.end: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated him at Buzakhah in 632 and he fled to Syria. He later repented, returned to Islam, and fought bravely for the Muslims at Qadisiyyah and Nahavand.
villains.note: From al-Tabari. He is remembered as a warning and as a hope: his false claim ended, and his repentance was accepted.
villains.lesson: The door of repentance stays open, even for one who claimed to be a prophet.

villains.name: Sajah
villains.title: The prophetess of Tamim
villains.relied: The tribes of Tamim and Taghlib
villains.deed: A woman of Banu Tamim who claimed prophethood after the Prophet's ﷺ death and marched on Yamamah, then made a pact with Musaylimah and married him.
villains.end: She turned back home after the pact, and her following melted away. Historians report she later accepted Islam and lived as a Muslim in Basra.

verse.to: nothing has been inspired to him

villains.note: From al-Tabari. Her return to Islam, in the time of Muawiyah, is reported by the historians.
villains.lesson: A claim built on alliances falls apart when the alliance does.

villains.name: Abu Lu'lu'ah
villains.title: Assassin of Umar
villains.deed: Fayruz, a Persian slave of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, stabbed Caliph Umar with a two-bladed dagger as he led the dawn prayer, then struck thirteen others as he fled.
villains.end: Trapped under a cloak, he killed himself. Umar died days later, thanking Allah that his killer was not a Muslim.
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari tells the killing in detail, from Amr ibn Maymun, who was in the prayer.
villains.lesson: Umar had asked Allah for martyrdom in the city of the Prophet ﷺ, and was given it.

villains.name: Abdullah ibn Saba'
villains.title: The stirrer of strife, in the histories
villains.deed: A Yemeni convert, the historians say, who toured the garrison towns spreading rumours against Uthman and extreme claims about Ali, and helped gather the rebels.
villains.end: Reports say Ali exiled him to al-Mada'in for his claims about him.
villains.note: Al-Tabari's account comes mostly through Sayf ibn Umar, a weak narrator. Some modern historians doubt that Ibn Saba' existed or played this role; others accept him. Treat the details with care.
villains.lesson: Check the news before you act on it (49:6).

villains.name: The rebels against Uthman
villains.title: Who besieged the caliph in his home
villains.relied: Rumours, forged letters and a mob
villains.deed: Bands from Egypt, Kufa and Basra, stirred by complaints and false letters, besieged Caliph Uthman in his house for weeks. He forbade the Companions to fight for him, and the rebels broke in and killed him as he read the Quran.
villains.end: His blood fell on the words 'Allah will be sufficient for you against them' (2:137). His killing opened the first civil war, and most of his killers died in the wars that followed.
villains.note: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. The Prophet ﷺ had given Uthman glad tidings of Paradise 'with a trial that will befall him' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3695).
villains.lesson: Uthman chose to die rather than let Muslims fight over him.

villains.name: The Khawarij
villains.title: Who declared Muslims disbelievers
villains.deed: Soldiers who left Ali after Siffin, called the arbitration disbelief, and then judged most Muslims disbelievers. They killed the Companion's son Abdullah ibn Khabbab and his pregnant wife on the road.
villains.end: Ali defeated them at Nahrawan in 658, as the Prophet ﷺ had foretold. Their remnants killed Ali and rose in revolt for centuries.
villains.note: The Prophet ﷺ described young men of foolish minds who recite the Quran but it goes no deeper than their throats (Sahih al-Bukhari 3611). Ali called their slogan 'a word of truth by which falsehood is intended' (Sahih Muslim). The killing of Ibn Khabbab is from al-Tabari.
villains.lesson: Extremism begins by judging others' faith and ends by spilling their blood.

villains.name: Ibn Muljam
villains.title: Assassin of Ali
villains.relied: Certainty that only his faction was Muslim
villains.deed: A Kharijite who struck Ali ibn Abi Talib with a poisoned sword at dawn prayer in the mosque of Kufa.
villains.end: Executed after Ali died of the wound. Ali asked that he be killed with one blow and not mutilated.
villains.note: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir.
villains.lesson: Extremism that calls Muslims disbelievers ends by killing the best of them.

villains.name: Ubaydullah ibn Ziyad
villains.title: The governor behind Karbala
villains.relied: Fear and the army of Kufa
villains.undone: Ibrahim ibn al-Ashtar at the River Khazir
villains.deed: Umayyad governor of Kufa who crushed support for Husayn, executed his envoy Muslim ibn Aqil, and sent the army that killed Husayn and his family at Karbala.
villains.end: When Husayn's head was brought to him he poked it with a stick, and Anas rebuked him. He was killed in battle at the River Khazir in 686.
villains.note: The scene with Husayn's head is in Sahih al-Bukhari. Sunni scholars hold the killing of Husayn to be a grave crime and a grief for the whole Ummah.
villains.lesson: Anas reminded him whose face that was: the one most like the Prophet ﷺ.

villains.name: al-Mukhtar al-Thaqafi
villains.title: The liar of Thaqif
villains.relied: Vengeance for Husayn, and claims of revelation
villains.deed: He took Kufa in the name of avenging Husayn and hunted down his killers, among them Ibn Ziyad. The historians report that he then claimed Jibril came to him, and spoke in rhymed prophecies.
villains.end: Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr besieged him in Kufa and he was killed in 687.

verse.to: nothing has been inspired to him

villains.note: The Prophet ﷺ foretold 'a liar and a destroyer' from Thaqif (Sahih Muslim 2545). Asma' bint Abi Bakr said 'the liar we have seen'; al-Nawawi and other scholars say she meant al-Mukhtar. His claims of revelation come from the historians.
villains.lesson: A just cause does not make a false claim true.

villains.name: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf
villains.title: The destroyer of Thaqif
villains.deed: Umayyad governor who besieged Makkah, struck the Kaaba with catapults and killed Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr in 692. In Iraq he ruled by fear and killed thousands, among them the great scholar Sa'id ibn Jubayr.
villains.end: He died in 714, months after Sa'id. His rule also saw dots and vowel marks added to the Quran's script and Sindh opened by his kinsman Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, but scholars remember him as the 'destroyer' the Prophet ﷺ foretold.
villains.note: Asma' bint Abi Bakr told al-Hajjaj to his face that he was the destroyer (Sahih Muslim 2545). Most scholars count him a tyrant and a great sinner, not a disbeliever. Anas told those who complained of him to be patient (Sahih al-Bukhari 7068).
villains.lesson: Asma', old and blind, told the most feared man in the empire the truth to his face.

villains.name: Abu Tahir al-Jannabi
villains.title: Who stole the Black Stone
villains.deed: Leader of the Qarmatians. He attacked Makkah during Hajj, killed pilgrims inside the Haram, threw bodies into Zamzam, and carried the Black Stone off to Bahrain.
villains.end: He died of disease in 944. The Black Stone came home in 951, after 22 years away.
villains.note: Ibn Kathir, al-Bidaya wan-Nihaya.
villains.lesson: Even the Kaaba's darkest year ended with the Stone back in its place.

villains.name: Hasan-i Sabbah
villains.title: Lord of Alamut
villains.relied: A mountain fortress and sworn killers
villains.deed: He seized the fortress of Alamut in the mountains of Persia in 1090. His followers became known as the Assassins, killing viziers, princes and scholars, beginning, the chroniclers say, with Nizam al-Mulk in 1092.
villains.end: He died in Alamut in 1124. His fortresses held for over a century, until Hulagu's Mongols took them in 1256.
villains.note: From Ibn al-Athir and Juvayni, who saw Alamut's library. The tales of hashish and a garden of paradise are later legends, mostly through Marco Polo. This entry is about one man's campaign of murder, not any community today.
villains.lesson: Whoever kills a soul unjustly, it is as if he had slain all mankind (5:32).

villains.name: Pope Urban II
villains.title: Who preached the First Crusade
villains.deed: At Clermont in 1095 he called the knights of Europe to march east and take Jerusalem, promising forgiveness of sins to those who went.
villains.end: The Crusaders took Jerusalem in 1099 and killed much of its Muslim and Jewish population. Urban died two weeks later, before the news reached Rome.
villains.note: His speech survives in several differing accounts by chroniclers. Ibn al-Athir describes the killing in al-Aqsa.
villains.lesson: Eighty-eight years later Salahuddin retook the city and spared its people.

villains.name: Reynald of Chatillon
villains.title: Raider of the pilgrims
villains.relied: The castle of Kerak and broken truces
villains.deed: A Crusader lord who plundered Hajj caravans in truce time and sent ships down the Red Sea to raid towards Makkah and Madinah.
villains.end: Captured at Hattin in 1187. Salahuddin had sworn to kill him and did so with his own hand.
villains.note: Ibn al-Athir and Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad, who was in Salahuddin's tent.
villains.lesson: Fulfil the covenant of Allah when you have made it (16:91).

villains.name: Hulagu
villains.title: Destroyer of Baghdad
villains.deed: The Mongol prince who sacked Baghdad, killed the caliph and a vast part of the city, and threw its libraries into the Tigris.
villains.end: His army was stopped by the Mamluks at Ain Jalut in 1260. He died in 1265.
villains.note: Ibn Kathir and Rashid al-Din.
villains.lesson: Within forty years, the Mongols of Persia had become Muslim themselves.

villains.name: Tomas de Torquemada
villains.title: Grand Inquisitor of Spain
villains.relied: The stake and the torture chamber
villains.deed: First head of the Spanish Inquisition under Ferdinand and Isabella. He hunted converts accused of secretly keeping their old faith, and pushed for the expulsion of Spain's Jews in 1492.
villains.end: He died in 1498. After him the Inquisition turned on the Muslims of Spain, who were forced to convert and finally expelled in 1609.
villains.note: Historians differ on how many were burned in his years; many estimates are around two thousand. The forced conversion of Spain's Muslims began in 1499-1502, after his death.

against.name: the Jews and Muslims of Spain

villains.lesson: There is no compulsion in religion (2:256).

villains.name: Vasco da Gama
villains.title: Who burned the pilgrim ship
villains.deed: On his second voyage to India in 1502, he captured the Miri, a ship carrying pilgrims home from Makkah. The passengers offered their wealth for their lives; he took the cargo and set the ship on fire with them aboard.
villains.end: Hundreds of men, women and children died. Portuguese fleets went on to attack Muslim ports and shipping across the Indian Ocean for a century.
villains.note: Told by the Portuguese eyewitness Tome Lopes, and by Zayn al-Din al-Ma'bari in Tuhfat al-Mujahidin. The number of dead varies in the sources.
villains.lesson: The Quran guards the safety of those travelling to the Sacred House (5:2).

villains.name: The Dajjal
villains.title: The false messiah
villains.relied: False wonders: rain on command, a paradise that is fire
villains.deed: One-eyed, with 'kafir' written between his eyes for every believer to read. He will claim to be lord, bring a false paradise and a false fire, and cross the whole earth except Makkah and Madinah.
villains.end: Isa ibn Maryam will descend and kill him at the gate of Ludd.
villains.note: Every prophet warned of him. Sahih Muslim 158 names him among three signs after which faith no longer benefits, as 6:158 describes. His story and his end are in Sahih Muslim 2937a.
villains.lesson: Every prophet warned of him. Muslims seek refuge from his trial in every prayer.

villains.name: Yajuj and Majuj
villains.title: The nations behind the wall
villains.deed: Countless peoples held back by Dhul-Qarnayn's wall of iron and copper. Released near the end, they will drink lakes dry, and Isa will shelter the believers on the mountain.
villains.end: Allah will send a worm into their necks, and they will die all at once, like a single soul.
villains.note: Named twice in the Quran. Their end is in Sahih Muslim.
villains.lesson: Numbers are nothing against the command of Allah.

villains.name: The thirty liars
villains.title: False prophets foretold
villains.relied: The claim to be a messenger of Allah
villains.deed: The Prophet ﷺ foretold that before the Hour about thirty liars would appear, each claiming to be a messenger of Allah.
villains.end: Musaylimah, al-Aswad, Tulayhah and Sajah were among the first. Every claimant since has failed, because Muhammad ﷺ is the last of the prophets (33:40).
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari. Scholars such as Ibn Hajar understood it of claimants who gained a following, not every person who ever made the claim.
villains.lesson: After the last Prophet ﷺ, a claim to new prophethood is its own disproof.

villains.name: The Sufyani
villains.title: A tyrant of the last days, in weak reports
villains.when: Before the Hour, in some reports
villains.undone: The earth that swallows his army, in the reports
villains.deed: Some narrations speak of a tyrant descended from Abu Sufyan who will rise in Syria, spill much blood, and send an army against a man who takes refuge at the Kaaba.
villains.end: Authentic hadith say an army marching on the Kaaba will be swallowed by the earth in the desert. Some later reports name its sender the Sufyani.
villains.note: The narrations that name the Sufyani, in al-Hakim's Mustadrak and Nu'aym ibn Hammad's al-Fitan, are weak by the hadith scholars' standards. The swallowed army is authentic (Sahih al-Bukhari 2118). Some commentators connect 34:51 to it.

against.name: the one who takes refuge at the Kaaba

villains.lesson: The scholars kept weak reports apart from sound ones, even about the end of time.

villains.name: Dhul-Suwayqatayn
villains.title: Who will tear down the Kaaba
villains.deed: A man from Abyssinia 'with two thin shins' who will pull the Kaaba down stone by stone.
villains.end: It is among the last signs before the Hour.
villains.note: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.
villains.lesson: Everything on earth will pass; only the Face of your Lord remains (55:26–27).
